metadata.scope: e_nusantara (203 baronies across k_kabisay-an, k_liuqiu, k_lusung, k_maluku, k_ruucuu, k_sulawesi)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_PHI_Butuan.first_mention_attestation: 1001 CE (Song Shi record of a Butuan tributary mission to the Song court on March 17, 1001 CE; also attested as But-wan on the 10th–12th century CE Butuan Ivory Seal)

morphemes.translation: mangosteen-related sour fruit tree (Garcinia morella / Garcinia binucao)

b_PHI_Butuan.etymology_analysis: Commonly derived from batuan, a sour fruit-bearing tree native to Mindanao, or alternatively from an early chief Datu Bantuan; attested in Song dynasty records (1001 CE) as Púduān (蒲端) and in Kawi script on the Butuan Ivory Seal as But-wan.

b_PHI_Cabadbaran.first_mention_attestation: 1867 CE (Spanish colonial records of the reduction 'La Reunión de Cabarbaran')
b_PHI_Cabadbaran.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Visayan/Butuanon root badbad ('to untie' or 'release'), with locative circumfix ka-...-an, traditionally linked to untying captives or 'badbaran sa kawad-on' ('release from want'). First recorded in Spanish reduction records in 1867 CE.

b_PHI_Baganga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; recorded during the Spanish colonial period (exact first year unverified in retrieved sources)

morphemes.translation: thorny plum-like fruit bush (or wide river mouth)

b_PHI_Baganga.etymology_analysis: Locally attributed either to a thorny bush bearing plum-like fruits abundant at the time of Spanish arrival, or to a local term referring to the wide mouth of the river traversing the town.

b_PHI_Agusan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; indigenous hydronym recorded in the Spanish colonial era
b_PHI_Agusan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the local word agasan ('where the water flows'), directly naming the Agusan River that drains northeastern Mindanao into Butuan Bay.

b_PHI_Surigao.first_mention_attestation: 1543 CE (recorded in early Spanish accounts of northeastern Mindanao / Caraga following the 1521 Magellan sighting and the 1543 Villalobos expedition; spelled Suligao / Surigao in 16th–17th century CE Spanish chronicles)

morphemes.translation: spring or rushing water current (or from suroy 'to roam/visit')

b_PHI_Surigao.etymology_analysis: Coastal toponym of northeastern Mindanao traditionally derived from Visayan/Surigaonon sulig ('to spring forth / strong current', referring to the Surigao Strait currents) or suroy ('to visit'). First documented in Spanish accounts of Mindanao in the mid-16th century CE.

b_PHI_Dinagat.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; indigenous island name documented in the Spanish colonial era
b_PHI_Dinagat.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Visayan root dagat ('sea') with the infix -in-, meaning 'of the sea' or 'like the sea', referring to Dinagat Island off northeastern Mindanao.

b_PHI_Siargao.first_mention_attestation: 1543 CE (first European sighting by Spanish navigator Bernardo de la Torre aboard San Juan de Letrán, charted as Isla de las Palmas; indigenous name from Visayan siargaw)
b_PHI_Siargao.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Visayan term siargaw or saliargaw (Premna odorata), a coastal tree/mangrove species native to Siargao Island.

b_PHI_Tandag.first_mention_attestation: 1609 CE (Spanish missionary arrival and stone fort construction at Tandag under Fr. Juan de la Vega)
b_PHI_Tandag.etymology_analysis: Attributed in local tradition to a vernacular term meaning 'lost' (or Manobo 'to cut/sever'). Spanish missionaries established a fort at Tandag in 1609 CE, and it became the capital of Caraga in 1650 CE.

b_PHI_Magugpo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; indigenous Mandaya/Mansaka settlement name in Davao del Norte predating its 1941 CE municipal renaming to Tagum
b_PHI_Magugpo.etymology_analysis: From Mandaya/Mansaka mago (a species of tall tree) and ugpo ('very high'), referring to a towering native tree at the original settlement site that later became Tagum City in Davao del Norte.

b_PHI_Mati.first_mention_attestation: 1903 CE (declared a municipality on October 29, 1903 CE under Organic Act No. 21; name derived from Mandaya Maa-ti)
b_PHI_Mati.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Mandaya word maa-ti, referring to the town's creek that easily dries up during dry weather.

b_PHI_Kuambog.first_mention_attestation: 1953 CE (Executive Order No. 596 of May 28, 1953 CE, designating Barrio Cuambog as the seat of the newly created municipality of Mabini)

morphemes.translation: a tree species of the family Dilleniaceae

b_PHI_Kuambog.etymology_analysis: Former name (spelled Cuambog) of Mabini, Davao de Oro, named after a local tree species of the family Dilleniaceae.

b_PHI_Malita.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; coastal municipality in Davao Occidental formally organized in 1936 CE

morphemes.translation: suitcase (adapted phonologically as Malita in local tradition)

b_PHI_Malita.etymology_analysis: Municipality in Davao Occidental whose name is locally explained via a folk etymology from Spanish maleta ('suitcase'), linked to a late-19th/early-20th-century river-crossing incident involving settler Mariano Peralta.

b_PHI_Glan.first_mention_attestation: 1914 CE (settlement founded by Visayan colonists arriving on October 8, 1914 CE; municipality created July 27, 1949 CE)

morphemes.translation: local toponym associated with a river or settlement

b_PHI_Glan.etymology_analysis: Settlement established in 1914 CE by Christianized Visayan settlers from Cebu; the name Glan is an indigenous local toponym of uncertain etymology.

b_PHI_Sarangani.first_mention_attestation: 1521 CE (noted by Antonio Pigafetta from the 1521 CE Magellan expedition and on his ca. 1525 CE chart; later reached in 1543 CE by the Ruy López de Villalobos expedition, who named it Antonia).

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym for the island off southern Mindanao

b_PHI_Sarangani.etymology_analysis: Indigenous toponym for Sarangani Island off the southern tip of Mindanao, documented in early 16th-century European charts and the 1543 CE Villalobos expedition.

b_PHI_Bagua_Inged.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; historic Maguindanaon settlement district in Cotabato along the Rio Grande de Mindanao

morphemes.translation: local district and settlement name in Cotabato

b_PHI_Bagua_Inged.etymology_analysis: Maguindanaon compound combining Bagua (a historic district of Cotabato City) with inged ('settlement, town, or homeland'), denoting a traditional Maguindanaon community in the Pulangi delta.

b_PHI_Malaybalay.first_mention_attestation: 1877 CE (June 15, 1877 CE accord between the Spanish government and Datu Mampaalong incorporating the settlement of Malaybalay into Misamis)

morphemes.translation: name of a spring along the Sawaga River (original meaning unknown; folk etymology 'few houses')

b_PHI_Malaybalay.etymology_analysis: Traced by historian Ludivina Opeña to the name of a spring along the Sawaga River (original meaning unknown), though often given the Cebuano folk etymology 'few houses'. First documented in Spanish records in 1877 CE.

b_PHI_Idalemen.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; indigenous ethnonym/toponym in Cotabato
b_PHI_Idalemen.etymology_analysis: Derived from dalem ('interior/deep/woods'), meaning 'people of the woods' or 'inland people', an indigenous subgroup name in northern Cotabato (Alamada area). Excluded from natural_proper_name as a directional/locator compound.

b_PHI_Tubok.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; historic coastal settlement (Tubok / Tuboc) in Malabang, Lanao del Sur, documented in modern and late-colonial Mindanao records

morphemes.translation: spring, bubbling water source, or point of emergence

b_PHI_Tubok.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Maranao/Iranun settlement name in coastal Malabang (Lanao del Sur) along Illana Bay, associated with a natural water spring or point of emergence on the corridor between the Maguindanao coast and Lake Lanao.

b_PHI_Masiu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; one of the four traditional principalities (Pat a Phangampong a Ranao) of Lanao (traditionally dated 16th–17th century CE)

morphemes.translation: traditional name of one of the four Lanao principalities (phangampong)

b_PHI_Masiu.etymology_analysis: Name of one of the four traditional Confederate States of Lanao (Pat a Phangampong a Ranao: Bayabao, Masiu, Unayan, and Balo-i), organized in the early Islamic/sultanate era around Lake Lanao.

b_PHI_Marahui.first_mention_attestation: 1895 CE (Spanish military campaigns against Fort Marahui in 1891–1895 CE)

morphemes.translation: reclining or bending (referring to water lilies or lake water at the Agus River outlet)

b_PHI_Marahui.etymology_analysis: Derived from Maranao rawi ('reclining'), referring to water lilies bending northward at the mouth of the Agus River or the reclining lake water. Spelled Marahui in late 19th-century Spanish documents.

b_PHI_Tagoloan.first_mention_attestation: 1500 CE (local historical tradition of Sharif Alawi establishing the Sultanate of Tagoloan around 1500 CE)

morphemes.translation: place of origin or settlement along the river

b_PHI_Tagoloan.etymology_analysis: Indigenous toponym shared by settlements in Lanao and Misamis Oriental; local traditions link it to a Maranao/Higaonon place of origin or settlement.

b_PHI_Tamontaka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; historic Maguindanaon riverine settlement on the southern branch of the Rio Grande de Mindanao, well documented in Spanish military and Jesuit mission records from 1861 CE onward

morphemes.translation: historic riverine settlement name in the lower Pulangi delta

b_PHI_Tamontaka.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Maguindanaon toponym of a prominent settlement on the southern distributary (Tamontaka River) of the Rio Grande de Mindanao in Cotabato, later the site of a major 19th-century Jesuit mission (1861 CE).

b_PHI_Lebak.first_mention_attestation: 1871 CE (first written record in Spanish colonial administration, establishing Lebac as a military district of Cotabato)
b_PHI_Lebak.etymology_analysis: From the Maguindanaon word lebak ('hollow'), describing the lowland coastal basin bordered by mountains to the east. First recorded in Spanish colonial records in 1871 CE.

b_PHI_Sapakan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; modern Maguindanaon barangay name in Rajah Buayan, Maguindanao del Sur

morphemes.translation: branch or fork (of a river or tree)

b_PHI_Sapakan.etymology_analysis: Maguindanaon toponym (from sapak 'branch/fork' + locative -an), designating the Poblacion barangay of Rajah Buayan in Maguindanao del Sur.

b_PHI_Makar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; modern port and district name in General Santos City

morphemes.translation: indigenous coastal/port toponym in Sarangani Bay

b_PHI_Makar.etymology_analysis: Indigenous coastal toponym in Sarangani Bay, preserved today as the Makar Port (Port of General Santos).

b_PHI_Matangal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; traditional Yakan and Sama toponym for Mount Matangal, Matangal Point, and the island of Basilan in the Sulu Archipelago

morphemes.translation: name of Mount Matangal and eastern cape of Basilan Island

b_PHI_Matangal.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Yakan/Sama toponym referring to Mount Matangal and Matangal Point on eastern Basilan, which served as a major maritime navigational landmark and an early pre-colonial name for Basilan Island.

b_PHI_Sulug.first_mention_attestation: 1304 CE (Chinese annal Nanhai Zhi; unelided Tausug form Sulug corresponding to modern Sūg / Spanish Sulu)
b_PHI_Sulug.etymology_analysis: Unelided Tausug form of Sūg ('sea current'), the indigenous endonym for Sulu and the Sulu Archipelago.

b_PHI_Pangutaran.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; documented in modern Sulu historiography (e.g., Saleeby 1908 CE) and local Islamic-era tradition
b_PHI_Pangutaran.eponym_details: Named after Shariff Pangutaran, a Muslim leader/settler (post-1380 CE Islamic era in Sulu) credited in local tradition with first settling the island.
b_PHI_Pangutaran.etymology_analysis: According to local Sulu tradition, named after Shariff Pangutaran, an early Muslim settler of the island (an earlier Malay name being Pulau Bangkuruan).

b_PHI_Tawi_Tawi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; recorded in early Spanish accounts as Tauitaui / Tavi-Tavi
b_PHI_Tawi_Tawi.etymology_analysis: Sinama adaptation of Malay jawi-jawi ('banyan tree'), abundant on Tawi-Tawi Island; an alternative local etymology derives it from Malay jauh ('far').

b_PHI_Bool.first_mention_attestation: 1565 CE (attested as Bo-ol / Bohol during Miguel López de Legazpi's 1565 CE expedition and blood compact with Datu Sikatuna; earlier sighted during Magellan's 1521 voyage)

morphemes.translation: name of a native tree/fruit giving rise to the island and polity name Bohol

b_PHI_Bool.etymology_analysis: Historic Visayan spelling (Bo-ol) of Bohol Island and its pre-colonial coastal polity in the central Visayas, traditionally derived from a native tree (bo-ol) growing near the early settlement of Bool (Tagbilaran).

b_PHI_Sugbu.first_mention_attestation: 1521 CE (recorded by Antonio Pigafetta as 'Zubu' / 'Çubu' during Magellan's arrival in April 1521 CE)

morphemes.translation: to wade or walk in shallow water

b_PHI_Sugbu.etymology_analysis: Pre-colonial indigenous name of Cebu City/Rajahnate of Cebu, from Cebuano sugbú ('to wade or dive into water', referring to shallow coastal waters where travelers waded ashore).

b_PHI_Siaro.first_mention_attestation: 1521 CE (Antonio Pigafetta's account of the southeastern coast of Cebu as 'Sialo', later documented in Augustinian parish records of 1599 CE)

morphemes.translation: historical chiefdom and coastal district of southeastern Cebu

b_PHI_Siaro.etymology_analysis: Variant of Sialo, a pre-colonial coastal settlement/chiefdom in southeastern Cebu (around modern Carcar/Valladolid), recorded by Pigafetta in 1521 CE and in 1599 CE Augustinian records.

b_PHI_Katugasan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; pre-colonial indigenous name of Siquijor Island documented in post-contact accounts
b_PHI_Katugasan.etymology_analysis: Pre-colonial name of Siquijor Island, from Visayan ka- + tugas ('molave tree') + -an, meaning 'place abundant in molave trees'.

b_PHI_Binalbagan.first_mention_attestation: 1573 CE (documented as one of the earliest native settlements and Spanish encomiendas/towns organized on Negros Island after Legazpi's 1565 arrival)

morphemes.translation: to break, shatter, or split (or bamboo pole/log)

b_PHI_Binalbagan.etymology_analysis: Hiligaynon/Visayan toponym in Negros Occidental derived from the root balbag ('to break/shatter') with the circumfix -in-...-an; recorded among the oldest coastal settlements of Negros in 1573 CE.

b_PHI_Ilog.first_mention_attestation: 1584 CE (founded as a town by Augustinian friars Gerónimo Marín and Francisco Bustos on May 16, 1584 CE)
b_PHI_Ilog.etymology_analysis: From Tagalog ilog ('river'), reportedly suggested by a Tagalog guide accompanying Spanish colonizers because the settlement is encircled by the Hilabangan River.

b_PHI_Dananguet.first_mention_attestation: 1572 CE (recorded as 'Dananguet' by Diego López Povedano in 1572 CE, prior to the 1734 CE spelling 'Dumaguete')

morphemes.translation: early form of Dumaguete (from dagit 'to snatch/swoop')

b_PHI_Dananguet.etymology_analysis: 16th-century name of Dumaguete recorded by Diego López Povedano in 1572 CE, linked to Cebuano dagit/dumaguet ('to snatch' or 'to swoop').

b_PHI_Nabingkalan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; pre-Spanish settlement name in Negros Occidental (later San Carlos City)

morphemes.translation: traditional name of a Negrito chieftain's daughter

b_PHI_Nabingkalan.etymology_analysis: Former name of San Carlos, Negros Occidental; local tradition derives it from Nabingka, the daughter of an indigenous Negrito chieftain.

b_PHI_Irong_Irong.first_mention_attestation: 1569 CE (recorded in early Spanish accounts of Panay following Miguel López de Legazpi's relocation to the island in 1569 CE; ancestor of the name Iloilo)
b_PHI_Irong_Irong.etymology_analysis: Reduplicated Hiligaynon/Kinaray-a form irong-irong ('nose-like'), describing the nose-shaped tongue of land formed by the Iloilo and Batiano rivers on southeastern Panay; later Spanish adaptation yielded 'Iloilo'.

b_PHI_Hamtik.first_mention_attestation: 1790 CE (established as the first capital of Antique politico-military province in 1790 CE; pre-Spanish district name Hantik)
b_PHI_Hamtik.etymology_analysis: From Kinaray-a hamtik/hantik, a species of large ants abundant in the area; Hispanicized as Hantique and Antique.

b_PHI_Akean.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; pre-Spanish Panay district (sakup) documented in post-contact sources
b_PHI_Akean.etymology_analysis: Named after the Akean (Aklan) River, from Aklanon akae ('to boil/froth') + -an, meaning 'where there is boiling or frothing' due to the river's turbulent current.

b_PHI_Himal-os.first_mention_attestation: 1581 CE (Spanish settlement established on Guimaras around 1581 CE under Governor Gonzalo Ronquillo de Peñalosa; earlier native name Himal-os)

morphemes.translation: pre-colonial indigenous name of Guimaras Island

b_PHI_Himal-os.etymology_analysis: Pre-colonial indigenous name of Guimaras Island, located between Panay and Negros.

b_PHI_Catarman.first_mention_attestation: c. 1616 CE (organized as a Spanish colonial pueblo in Northern Samar in the early 17th century CE, c. 1616–1622, following Jesuit missionary arrival on Samar in 1596 CE)

morphemes.translation: sharp, blade-like (referring to sharp coastal rocks or local flora)

b_PHI_Catarman.etymology_analysis: Waray-Waray toponym in Northern Samar formed from ka-...-an + tarom ('sharp'), traditionally linked to sharp rocks/reefs along the Catarman coast or river mouth; first formally organized in the early 17th century CE.

b_PHI_Catbalogan.first_mention_attestation: 1596 CE (founded in October 1596 CE by Spanish Jesuit priests under Fr. Francisco de Otazo)

morphemes.translation: coastal shrub or Strychnos ignatii vine

b_PHI_Catbalogan.etymology_analysis: Derived from Waray katbalaugan ('place of balaug shrubs / refuge for seafarers') or catbalongaan ('place where the catbalonga plant, Strychnos ignatii, grows'). Founded as a Jesuit mission in 1596 CE.

b_PHI_Borongan.first_mention_attestation: 1604 CE (Spanish missionary history of Borongan beginning in 1604 CE)
b_PHI_Borongan.etymology_analysis: Derived from Waray borong ('fog') + locative -an, referring to the morning fog covering the surrounding mountains.

b_PHI_Baybay.first_mention_attestation: 1620 CE (established as a Jesuit mission town on western Leyte c. 1620 CE; known as a native coastal settlement during 16th-century Spanish contact in the Visayas)
b_PHI_Baybay.etymology_analysis: From Visayan (Cebuano/Waray) baybay meaning 'shore' or 'seashore', describing the coastal settlement on the western shore of Leyte facing the Camotes Sea.

b_PHI_Kankabatok.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; original settlement name of Tacloban documented in local colonial-era history
b_PHI_Kankabatok.etymology_analysis: Original name of Tacloban (facing Cancabato Bay) before being renamed after the taklub bamboo fish trap.

b_PHI_Panamao.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; recorded in early Spanish accounts as 'Isla de Panamao' (before 'Biliran' was adopted in the late 17th–18th century CE)

morphemes.translation: ethnic fishing net, or the northern volcano on Biliran Island

b_PHI_Panamao.etymology_analysis: Early Spanish-era name for Biliran Island (Isla de Panamao), referring to its northernmost mountain/volcano (Mount Panamao) or an ethnic fishing net.

b_PHI_Tukuran.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; strategic isthmus settlement in Zamboanga del Sur documented in late-19th-century CE Spanish military records (Fort Alfonso XIII, 1891 CE)
b_PHI_Tukuran.etymology_analysis: Derived from Visayan/Cebuano tukod ('to build' or 'prop up') plus locative -an ('place of construction'), located on the narrow Zamboanga isthmus linking Illana Bay and Panguil Bay.

b_PHI_Kumalarang.first_mention_attestation: 1417 CE (Ming Shilu / Ming Shi record of Eunuch Zhang Qian sent on December 15, 1417 CE to King Kanlai Ipentun of Kumalarang, Gǔmǎlàlǎng 古麻剌朗)

morphemes.translation: indigenous name of the Subanon kingdom on Dumanquilas Bay

b_PHI_Kumalarang.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Subanon kingdom name, attested in Ming Chinese records (Ming Shilu and Ming Shi) beginning in 1417 CE as Gǔmǎlàlǎng (古麻剌朗).

b_PHI_Bolong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; former town merged into Zamboanga City in the modern/colonial era

morphemes.translation: local barangay and former town name east of Zamboanga

b_PHI_Bolong.etymology_analysis: Coastal settlement and former town east of Zamboanga City, now a barangay of Zamboanga City.

b_taiwan_new_1.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; indigenous Sakizaya/Amis settlement and regional name Kiray / Kilai (transcribed in Chinese as 奇萊 Qilai) for the Hualien plain in eastern Taiwan, recorded in Qing-era gazetteers

morphemes.translation: indigenous name of the Sakizaya settlement and Hualien plain (奇萊)

b_taiwan_new_1.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Austronesian name (Sakizaya/Amis Kiray, Hokkien Kî-lâi, Mandarin Qílái 奇萊) for the Hualien plain in eastern Taiwan, used until the early 20th century before Japanese authorities replaced it with Karenkō (Hualien).

b_taiwan_new_2.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; indigenous autonym of the Amis people of eastern Taiwan, first recorded in modern ethnographic and Qing/Japanese-era documentation

morphemes.translation: human being, people of our kind

b_taiwan_new_2.etymology_analysis: Endonym of the northern and central Amis Austronesian people of eastern Taiwan (Hualien and Taitung), meaning 'human' or 'people of our kind', contrasting with the exonym Amis ('north').

b_taiwan_new_3.first_mention_attestation: 1632 CE (recorded as Cabaran / Cabarán in Spanish colonial documents of northern Taiwan from 1632 CE, later as Cabalang in Dutch VOC records and 噶瑪蘭 Gamalan in Qing sources)

morphemes.translation: people of the flatland, plains dwellers

b_taiwan_new_3.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Austronesian ethnonym and territorial name of the Kavalan people of northeastern Taiwan's Lanyang (Yilan) Plain, meaning 'people of the flatlands'; first documented in 1632 CE Spanish Formosa records.

b_taiwan_changhua.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; indigenous Babuza/Hoanya settlement name Poasoa (rendered in Hokkien/Chinese as 半線 Pòaⁿ-sòaⁿ / Banxian) in central-western Taiwan, documented in 17th-century Dutch VOC and early Qing sources prior to the 1723 CE renaming to Changhua

morphemes.translation: indigenous settlement name in Changhua (transcribed as 半線 Pòaⁿ-sòaⁿ)

b_taiwan_changhua.etymology_analysis: Pre-Qing Plains Indigenous (Babuza/Hoanya) settlement name in west-central Taiwan, phonetically transliterated into Taiwanese Hokkien as Pòaⁿ-sòaⁿ (半線, Mandarin Banxian) before Qing authorities established Changhua County there in 1723 CE.

b_taiwan_miaoli.first_mention_attestation: Standardized as Miaoli (苗栗) when Miaoli County was established in 1889 CE during late Qing rule, modifying earlier Qing-era Hakka transliterations (貓裏, 貓裡, 貓里).
b_taiwan_miaoli.etymology_analysis: Coined using two Hakka syllables (originally 貓貍/貓裏) approximating the Taokas word 'Pali' (or 'Bari'), meaning 'plain'. Modified to 苗栗 (Miaoli) in 1889 CE.

b_taiwan_taipei.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; indigenous Basay/Ketagalan toponym Hoba / Hobe for the Tamsui estuary in northern Taiwan, rendered in Hokkien/Chinese as 滬尾 (Hō͘-bé / Huwei) in Qing-era records from the 17th–18th centuries CE
b_taiwan_taipei.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Basay/Ketagalan place name meaning 'stream mouth' or 'estuary', designating the port area of modern Tamsui at the mouth of the Tamsui River in northern Taiwan and transcribed in Hokkien as 滬尾 (Hō͘-bé).

b_taiwan_new_4.first_mention_attestation: Indigenous Atayal toponym with no pre-modern datable first written mention; Wulai's hot springs were documented in Japanese colonial records in 1903 CE.
b_taiwan_new_4.etymology_analysis: From the Atayal word 'ulay' (hot/boiling water), referring to the natural geothermal hot springs in the Nanshi River valley, later Sinicized as Wulai (烏來).

b_taiwan_chiayi.first_mention_attestation: 1624 CE (documented in Dutch East India Company administrative and missionary accounts from 1624–1628 CE onward as the Plains Indigenous people and territory of southwestern Taiwan; earlier visited without the ethnonym by Chen Di in 1603 CE)

morphemes.translation: indigenous autonym ('people / inland people') of southwestern Taiwan

b_taiwan_chiayi.etymology_analysis: Autonym of the Siraya Austronesian Plains Indigenous people inhabiting the southwestern Chianan Plain of Taiwan (modern Tainan and Chiayi regions), extensively recorded in 17th-century Dutch VOC sources.

b_taiwan_kaohsiung.first_mention_attestation: 1603 CE (attested as 打狗 Dagou / Takau in Chen Di's late Ming account Dongfan Ji of 1603 CE, and as Tancoia / Takow in 17th-century Dutch VOC records, before being renamed Kaohsiung in 1920 CE)

morphemes.translation: bamboo forest (transcribed in Hokkien as 打狗 Tá-káu)

b_taiwan_kaohsiung.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Makatao/Siraya toponym meaning 'bamboo forest', naming the historic harbor settlement of modern Kaohsiung in southwestern Taiwan; transcribed in Chinese as 打狗 (Takau/Dagou) from at least 1603 CE until 1920 CE.

b_taiwan_pingtung.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; indigenous Makatao village name Akau (transcribed in Hokkien/Chinese as 阿猴 A-kâu / Ahou) in southern Taiwan, documented in early Qing records from the late 17th–18th centuries CE prior to the 1920 CE renaming to Pingtung

morphemes.translation: forest, wooded area (transcribed in Hokkien as 阿猴 A-kâu)

b_taiwan_pingtung.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Makatao settlement name meaning 'forest' in southern Taiwan, rendered in Taiwanese Hokkien as 阿猴 (A-kâu) during Qing rule before being renamed Pingtung in 1920 CE.

b_PHI_Cagayan.first_mention_attestation: First documented by Spanish expeditions in 1572 CE when Juan de Salcedo explored the northern Luzon coast; civil government of Cagayan established in 1583 CE.
b_PHI_Cagayan.etymology_analysis: Linguists derive 'Cagayan' from an ancient Philippine root (cognate with Ilocano 'karayan' and 'kagayan') meaning 'river', referring to the Cagayan River (folk etymology links it to the 'tagay' plant). In-game repo state uses 'Kagajândal'.

b_PHI_Engano.first_mention_attestation: Spanish colonial cape name with no confirmed exact first-mention year; the Cape Engaño Lighthouse on Palaui Island was constructed in 1888–1892 CE.
b_PHI_Engano.etymology_analysis: Named 'Cabo Engaño' (Cape Deception/Illusion) by Spanish seafarers, traditionally attributed to their astonishment at the cape's natural beauty on Palaui Island at the northeastern tip of Luzon.

b_PHI_Ilongot.first_mention_attestation: Indigenous ethnolinguistic name (also Bugkalot) with no datable pre-867 or single earliest written mention; documented in Spanish and American colonial ethnography.
b_PHI_Ilongot.etymology_analysis: Exonymic/ethnonymic designation for the Bugkalot people inhabiting the southern Sierra Madre and Caraballo Mountains of Luzon, formed with the locative prefix 'i-' (people of).

b_PHI_Tagalao.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in standard historical sources; likely a mod-adapted or obscure local/map spelling within the Kasiguranin (Aurora/Isabela) area.
b_PHI_Tagalao.etymology_analysis: No verified historical or linguistic etymology found in Philippine gazetteers; appears in-game as the capital holding of c_PHI_kasiguranin ('Kasigurânin').

b_PHI_Kirino.first_mention_attestation: Created as Quirino Province on June 18, 1966 CE under Republic Act No. 4734, carved out of Nueva Vizcaya.
b_PHI_Kirino.eponym_details: Named after Elpidio Quirino (1890–1956 CE), sixth President of the Philippines (1948–1953 CE).

morphemes.translation: armed with a lance (surname of President Elpidio Quirino)

b_PHI_Kirino.etymology_analysis: Post-colonial administrative name honoring Philippine President Elpidio Quirino (1890–1956 CE), rendered phonetically in-game as 'Kirino'.

b_PHI_Palana.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1588 CE as a visita of Casiguran, and formally established as a pueblo on July 22, 1609 CE by Franciscan Fray Blas Palomino.
b_PHI_Palana.etymology_analysis: Local traditions derive 'Palanan' from Tagalog 'palanan' (preparation), inverted Agta 'nanatap' (catch), or Ibanag 'palanakko' (feeling of apprehension).

b_PHI_Apayo.first_mention_attestation: Established as the sub-province of Apayao in 1907 CE during the American colonial period; derived from the indigenous Isneg river-name 'apa'yaw'.
b_PHI_Apayo.etymology_analysis: From Cordilleran 'apa'yaw' (overtaking), referring to the swift-flowing upper Apayao-Abulug River system; Spaniards rendered it 'Apayao'. In-game repo state uses the county name 'Igorôt'.

b_PHI_Kalinga.first_mention_attestation: Indigenous/exonymic highland name with no datable pre-867 written mention; organized as a sub-province in 1907 CE.
b_PHI_Kalinga.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Ibanag and Gaddang noun 'kalinga' meaning 'enemy', 'fighter', or 'headtaker', applied as an exonym to the Cordillera highland people.

b_PHI_Benguet.first_mention_attestation: Organized as the first Philippine Civil Government under American rule in 1900 CE (following 19th-century Spanish military districts in the Cordillera).

morphemes.translation: edge, rim (referring to a valley/lake rim)

b_PHI_Benguet.etymology_analysis: From a Spanish mispronunciation of the native Cordilleran word 'benget' (edge/rim), originally applied to the La Trinidad valley settlement.

b_PHI_Babuyan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Pai-p'u-yen' (巴布延) in Zhao Rugua's Zhu Fan Zhi (1225 CE) as a northern island trading point associated with Ma-i.
b_PHI_Babuyan.etymology_analysis: Philippine locative formation from 'babuy' (pig/wild boar) + '-an' (place of), transcribed in 13th-century Chinese sources as Pai-p'u-yen (巴布延). In-game repo state uses 'Iwatan' (Ivatan).

b_PHI_Calayan.first_mention_attestation: A Spanish mission headquarters was established on Calayan Island in 1722 CE.
b_PHI_Calayan.etymology_analysis: From the Ibanag language, meaning 'place where laya (ginger) abounds', formed with the circumfix ka- ... -an.

b_PHI_Aparri.first_mention_attestation: Visited by Spanish conquistador Juan de Salcedo on June 29, 1572 CE during his exploration of northern Luzon; a church was erected in 1604 CE.
b_PHI_Aparri.etymology_analysis: Folk etymology derives 'Aparri' from Ibanag 'Aparrian' ('where priests resided'), referring to the Spanish friars who built the church in 1604 CE, though the coastal settlement already existed by 1572 CE.

b_PHI_Binalatongan.first_mention_attestation: Encountered by Spanish forces under Martín de Goiti and Juan de Salcedo in 1572 CE as the capital of Pangasinan (Caboloan); razed and renamed San Carlos in the 1760s.
b_PHI_Binalatongan.etymology_analysis: Derived from Pangasinan 'balatong' (mung bean) with locative affixation, meaning a place where mung beans grew abundantly. In-game repo state uses 'Pangasînan'.

b_PHI_Bolinao.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Spanish settlement by Captain Pedro Lombi in 1575 CE (the 1324 CE Odoric of Pordenone mass claim is rejected by modern scholars).
b_PHI_Bolinao.etymology_analysis: Folk etymology attributes the name to 'bolinao', the Tagalog/Bikol/Visayan term for the local anchovy ('monamon'), or alternatively to a phonetic adaptation of the 'pamulinawen' tree.

b_PHI_Pantabagan.first_mention_attestation: Founded on November 30, 1645 CE by Augustinian missionary Fr. Juan Alonzo de Abarca.
b_PHI_Pantabagan.etymology_analysis: Local tradition attributes 'Pantabangan' to Fr. Abarca's 1645 CE naming based on the indigenous groups' reaction upon tasting bread.

b_PHI_Sambala.first_mention_attestation: Derived from the ethnonym of the Sambal people, Hispanized as 'Zambales' in the late 16th century without a single verified earliest year for the form 'Sambala'.

morphemes.translation: indigenous ethnic group of western Luzon

b_PHI_Sambala.etymology_analysis: Ethnonymic toponym representing the homeland of the Sambal people along the western coast of Luzon (modern Zambales).

b_PHI_Bigan.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1574 CE by Spanish conquistador Juan de Salcedo (as Villa Fernandina), who recorded the native name as 'Bigan'.
b_PHI_Bigan.etymology_analysis: Recorded by Salcedo in 1574 CE as 'Bigan' after locals replied 'biga' (a taro-family plant) when asked what was growing on the riverbank; an alternative legend links it to Hokkien/Chinese 'bi-gan' (beautiful shore). In-game repo state uses 'Samtôi' (Samtoy).

b_PHI_Kandong.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as 'Candón' or 'Candon' in Spanish colonial records; no confirmed pre-867 or exact first-mention year.
b_PHI_Kandong.etymology_analysis: Either a Hispanicization of Ilocano 'kandong' (a native hardwood tree that served as a community meeting point) or named after Candón in Huelva, Spain.

b_PHI_Nagparitan.first_mention_attestation: Became a town under the name Nagpartian (earlier Nagparitan) in 1895 CE; renamed Burgos in 1914 CE after Fr. José Burgos.
b_PHI_Nagparitan.etymology_analysis: From Ilocano 'nagparitan' (place of prohibition), referring to early inhabitants who barred outsiders from settling; later altered by the Spanish to 'Nagpartian' (place of slaughter) and renamed Burgos in 1914 CE.

b_PHI_Tagbanwa.first_mention_attestation: Indigenous ethnonym of the Tagbanwa people of Palawan with no datable pre-867 written mention.
b_PHI_Tagbanwa.etymology_analysis: Indigenous endonym meaning 'people from our place/country' (taga-banwa). In-game repo state uses 'Sût-Palâwan' (South Palawan).

b_PHI_Pala_wan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Pa-lau-yu' / 'Pa-lao-yu' in Zhao Rugua's Zhu Fan Zhi (1225 CE) as one of the 'Three Islands' (San-su) associated with Ma-i; called 'Isla de Paragua' in Spanish records.

morphemes.translation: native plant or 'land of beautiful harbors'

b_PHI_Pala_wan.etymology_analysis: Debated origin: either from the local 'palaw' plant, Chinese 'Pa-lao-yu' (land of beautiful harbors) in 1225 CE, or related to Spanish 'Paragua' (umbrella-shaped island).

b_PHI_Balabac.first_mention_attestation: Documented in an April 1753 CE Spanish report noting Sulu's control over Palawan and Balabac.
b_PHI_Balabac.etymology_analysis: Evolved from 'Balabag', meaning 'cross-wise' in reference to the geographical orientation of the main island; the indigenous Molbog people originally called the area Molbog.

b_PHI_Taytay.first_mention_attestation: Formally founded as a Spanish town in 1623 CE; Antonio Pigafetta's 1521 CE chronicle earlier noted the northern Palawan coast.
b_PHI_Taytay.etymology_analysis: Derived from the local Philippine word 'taytay' meaning 'bridge' (or ridge/pathway).

b_PHI_Jamayan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Kia-ma-yen' / 'Jiamayan' in Zhao Rugua's Zhu Fan Zhi (1225 CE) as one of the 'Three Islands' (San-su) under Ma-i, identified with Calamian.
b_PHI_Jamayan.etymology_analysis: Song-era Chinese transcription ('Kia-ma-yen' / 'Jiamayan') of the Calamian Islands in northern Palawan, recorded in the 1225 CE Zhu Fan Zhi.

b_PHI_Cuyo.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Spanish settlement in 1622 CE; later fortified with Cuyo Church and Fort in 1680 CE.
b_PHI_Cuyo.etymology_analysis: Historic island settlement in the Sulu Sea between Palawan and Panay, center of the Cuyunon people.

b_PHI_Ibat.first_mention_attestation: Appears in Bicol oral/folkloric tradition (a settlement ruled by Gat Ibal) with no datable contemporary written attestation.
b_PHI_Ibat.etymology_analysis: Traditional Bikol toponym associated in local lore with Gat Ibal and the early Ibalon region. In-game repo state uses the county name 'Ibalong'.

b_PHI_Daet.first_mention_attestation: Pre-Hispanic Bikol settlement encountered by Spanish missionaries in the late 16th century (1500s CE), with no single verified exact first-mention year.

morphemes.translation: to make close, to bind together

b_PHI_Daet.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Bikol word 'dai-daitan' (to make close or bind), reflecting close-knit riverside communities.

b_PHI_Ibalon.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as the Spanish name for the Bicol region in the late 16th century (1570s CE), and as the setting of the 'Ibalong' folk epic published by Fray José Castaño in 1895 CE.

morphemes.translation: to bring to the other side

b_PHI_Ibalon.etymology_analysis: Variously interpreted in Bikol as deriving from 'ibalio' (to bring to the other side) or 'ibalon' (people from the other side). In-game repo state uses 'Baltogkirchen' (a German-flavored mod name referencing the epic hero Baltog).

b_PHI_Sorsogon.first_mention_attestation: Spanish-era Bikol toponym originating from 1570s CE contact accounts, with no single verified exact first-mention year.
b_PHI_Sorsogon.etymology_analysis: Traditional etymology derives 'Sorsogon' from Bikol 'solsogon' (follow the river upstream), spoken by locals directing Spanish explorers in the 1570s CE (alternative folk link to the sorsogon/balinad tree).

b_PHI_Katanduan.first_mention_attestation: First recorded by Spanish conquistadors in 1573 CE (initially as 'Isla de Cobos'), later Hispanicizing the indigenous name 'Katanduan' to 'Catanduanes'.
b_PHI_Katanduan.etymology_analysis: From Bikol 'katanduan' (place where the tandu beetle/tree thrives in abundance), Hispanicized as Catanduanes.

b_PHI_Pilila.first_mention_attestation: First Spanish missionary priests arrived in Pililla in 1572 CE (per NHCP historical marker); town autonomy was granted in 1583 CE.

morphemes.translation: rice paddy dike (parent town of Pila, Laguna)

b_PHI_Pilila.etymology_analysis: Originally 'Pilang Muntî' (Little Pila), translated into Spanish as 'Pililla' (Pila + diminutive '-illa'). In-game repo state uses the county name 'Kalilâjan' (Kalilayan).

b_PHI_Bondoc.first_mention_attestation: Geographic peninsula name in southeastern Quezon with Franciscan missions dating to the early 1600s CE; no single verified earliest written year for 'Bondoc'.
b_PHI_Bondoc.etymology_analysis: Named after the Bondoc Peninsula in Quezon Province, from Tagalog 'bundok' (mountain/upland).

b_PHI_Pulilu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'P'u-li-lu' / 'Pulilu' in Zhao Rugua's Zhu Fan Zhi (1225 CE), described as connected to the Three Islands (San-su) and producing rare coral.
b_PHI_Pulilu.etymology_analysis: 13th-century Chinese transcription ('Pulilu') of the Polillo Island polity off the eastern coast of Luzon, later Hispanicized as Polillo.

b_PHI_Malindig.first_mention_attestation: Indigenous Tagalog/Marinduque oronym (Mount Malindig) with no datable pre-867 written mention.
b_PHI_Malindig.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Malindig, the stratovolcano on Marinduque Island, from Tagalog/Visayan 'malindig'/'malindug' meaning 'standing tall' or 'elegant' (also the likely source of 'Marinduque').

b_PHI_Pinamalayan.first_mention_attestation: Organized as a permanent settlement in the 1800s CE under a Gobernadorcillo.

morphemes.translation: place where something was made known

b_PHI_Pinamalayan.etymology_analysis: From Tagalog 'ipinamalay' / 'pinamalayan' (place where it was made aware/known), linked in local tradition to settlers sighting Mindoro Island. In-game repo state uses the county name 'Mâ-Î' (Ma-i).

b_PHI_Mamburao.first_mention_attestation: Encountered during Juan de Salcedo's Spanish expedition to Mindoro in May 1570 CE.

morphemes.translation: historic coastal settlement name in Mindoro

b_PHI_Mamburao.etymology_analysis: Pre-Hispanic coastal settlement and trading/Moro stronghold on northwestern Mindoro, recorded by Spanish expeditions in 1570 CE.

b_PHI_Dongon.first_mention_attestation: Toponym for Dongon Point in Sablayan, Occidental Mindoro, with no datable pre-867 written mention.
b_PHI_Dongon.etymology_analysis: Named after Dongon Point, a headland south of Sablayan in Occidental Mindoro, itself derived from the 'dongon' (dungon) tree.

b_PHI_Bongabong.first_mention_attestation: Originally established in the 16th century CE as 'Binagao' (administered by Jesuits in the 17th century); the modern name 'Bongabong' dates to the American colonial era (early 20th century).
b_PHI_Bongabong.etymology_analysis: Earlier known as 'Binagao' (a Mangyan term for a big, turbulent river); local tradition attributes the modern name 'Bongabong' to the American era (from 'bunga' + gunshot 'bong').

b_PHI_Masbate.first_mention_attestation: First documented in Fray Martín de Rada's letter of July 1569 CE and the 1569 CE Spanish expedition under Captain Luis Enríquez de Guzmán.
b_PHI_Masbate.etymology_analysis: First recorded in 1569 CE Spanish accounts (also as 'Masbad'); folk etymology links it to 'masbat' or 'masa-bati' (mixing/kneading).

b_PHI_Ticao.first_mention_attestation: Spanish-era island toponym in Masbate; local San Jacinto history cites a 1603 CE settlement and English frigate passage, with no confirmed pre-867 mention.
b_PHI_Ticao.etymology_analysis: Island in Masbate Province along the Manila Galleon route (Ticao Pass), recorded in Spanish colonial navigation and mission accounts.

b_PHI_Donblon.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as 'Donblon' (alongside 'Lomlom') by Spanish chronicler Miguel de Loarca in Relación de las Islas Filipinas (1582 CE).

morphemes.translation: brooding hen sitting on eggs (traditional etymology)

b_PHI_Donblon.etymology_analysis: Spanish chronicler Miguel de Loarca recorded the island as 'Donblon' in 1582 CE, an intermediate form between 'Lomlom' (from Romblomanon 'nagalumyom', brooding hen) and modern 'Romblon'.

b_PHI_Tondo.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Tundun' in the Laguna Copperplate Inscription, dated Saka 822 (900 CE) — 33 years post-867 CE.
b_PHI_Tondo.etymology_analysis: First attested in 900 CE as 'Tundun' in the Laguna Copperplate Inscription (Old Tagalog/Old Malay), likely from 'tundok' or 'tundo' denoting elevated dry ground by the Pasig River delta.

b_PHI_Kapampangan.first_mention_attestation: 1571 CE, in Spanish colonial records establishing La Pampanga as the first Spanish province on Luzon.
b_PHI_Kapampangan.etymology_analysis: Derived from Kapampangan ka- + pampáng ('riverbank') + -an, denoting the people and territory along the banks of the Pampanga River; Spanish colonizers adapted it as La Pampanga in 1571 CE.

b_PHI_Maynila.first_mention_attestation: 1570 CE, in Spanish expedition accounts of Martín de Goiti's arrival at the fortified Tagalog polity of Maynila.
b_PHI_Maynila.etymology_analysis: From Tagalog may ('there is') + nilad (a mangrove shrub, Scyphiphora hydrophyllacea, growing along the Pasig River delta). Earlier 14th-century references to Saludung/Selurong (1365 CE Nagarakretagama) are also post-867 CE.

b_PHI_Batangan.first_mention_attestation: 1601 CE, in Spanish colonial records modifying the indigenous Tagalog settlement name Batangan into Batangas.
b_PHI_Batangan.etymology_analysis: From Tagalog batang ('log' or 'raft') + -an, referring to the numerous logs found in the Calumpang River or fishing rafts used on Taal Lake.

b_PHI_Binangonan.first_mention_attestation: 1621 CE, in Franciscan ecclesiastical records noting Binangonan's separation from Morong as an independent parish.
b_PHI_Binangonan.etymology_analysis: Derived from Tagalog bangon ('to rise') with the circumfix -in-...-an, meaning 'place where something rose' or 'place of awakening'.

b_IDO_Galiyao.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE, in the Old Javanese poem Nagarakretagama, which lists 'Galiao' (Pantar) among Majapahit's eastern dependencies.
b_IDO_Galiyao.etymology_analysis: Historical regional exonym/toponym attested as Galiao in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama, identified with Pantar Island in the Alor Archipelago.

b_IDO_Lembata.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (post-1511 CE), in early Portuguese maritime accounts of the Solor Archipelago and Lamalera whalers.

morphemes.translation: indigenous island name (also known as Lomblen)

b_IDO_Lembata.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Lamaholot island name, historically also rendered Lomblen or Kawela; no written attestation exists prior to 867 CE.

b_IDO_Alor.first_mention_attestation: 1522 CE, in Antonio Pigafetta's account of the Magellan expedition (as Mallua) and later 16th-century Portuguese/Dutch records.
b_IDO_Alor.etymology_analysis: Indigenous island name in the Alor Archipelago; lacks any contemporary written attestation before 867 CE.

b_IDO_Kodi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; indigenous domain, district, and Austronesian ethnolinguistic group in western Sumba, documented in Dutch colonial and ethnographic sources from the 19th–20th centuries CE

morphemes.translation: indigenous domain and ethnonym of westernmost Sumba

b_IDO_Kodi.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Sumbanese domain and ethnolinguistic name (also historically spelled Kudi) on the western tip of Sumba Island in East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia.

b_IDO_Melolo.first_mention_attestation: Modern/vernacular settlement name in East Sumba; no pre-modern written attestation (the Melolo urn-burial site was archaeologically excavated in the 1920s CE).
b_IDO_Melolo.etymology_analysis: Vernacular East Sumbanese toponym in the Rindi/Melolo coastal area, famous for prehistoric urn burials excavated in the 1920s CE but lacking any pre-867 CE written record.

b_IDO_Sawu.first_mention_attestation: 1756 CE, in Dutch East India Company (VOC) treaties negotiated by John Andrew Paravicini with rulers of Sawu, Rote, and Sumba.

morphemes.translation: indigenous name of Savu Island (adapted as Sawu/Sabu)

b_IDO_Sawu.etymology_analysis: From the indigenous Savunese endonym Hawu (Dou Hawu), rendered in Malay and Dutch as Sawu, Sabu, or Savu.

b_IDO_Larantuka.first_mention_attestation: c. 1600 CE (documented as a major Portuguese/Topass trading and Dominican missionary center in East Flores by c. 1600 CE, following earlier 16th-century Portuguese presence in the Solor-Flores strait)
b_IDO_Larantuka.etymology_analysis: Lamaholot toponym of the historic kingdom and port town at the eastern tip of Flores Island, traditionally glossed from laran ('road/path') + tuka ('middle'), i.e. 'the middle way' or midpoint along the Flores-Solor strait.

b_IDO_Endeh.first_mention_attestation: Late 16th century CE (1595 CE), in Portuguese Dominican and Dutch accounts of central Flores and the rajadom of Endeh.
b_IDO_Endeh.etymology_analysis: Indigenous central Flores toponym and ethnonym (historically spelled Endeh in colonial sources), attested only from the early modern period.

b_IDO_Bajo.first_mention_attestation: Modern/vernacular settlement name (Labuan Bajo) in western Flores; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_IDO_Bajo.etymology_analysis: Short form of Labuan Bajo ('anchorage of the Bajau'), named after the Sama-Bajau seafaring communities who settled the western coast of Flores.

b_IDO_Wetar.first_mention_attestation: 17th century CE, in early Dutch and Portuguese Maluku cartography and colonial records.
b_IDO_Wetar.etymology_analysis: Indigenous island name in the Barat Daya group north of Timor; unattested in written sources before the early modern colonial era.

b_IDO_Barat_Daya.first_mention_attestation: Modern Indonesian geographic/administrative designation ('Southwest Islands'); no pre-modern written attestation.
b_IDO_Barat_Daya.etymology_analysis: Modern Indonesian directional compound barat daya ('southwest'), referring to the Southwestern Islands of Maluku.

b_IDO_Tanimbar.first_mention_attestation: 1629 CE, when Dutch navigators first visited the Tanimbar Islands (subsequently claimed by the VOC in 1639 CE).
b_IDO_Tanimbar.etymology_analysis: Related to local Tanimbarese forms tanempar, tanebar, and tnebar meaning 'stranded', referring to groups arriving from across eastern Indonesia.

b_IDO_Kupang.first_mention_attestation: 1613 CE (first explicitly recorded in Dutch East India Company accounts in 1613 CE when Apollonius Schotte contacted the Raja of Kupang on western Timor)

morphemes.translation: indigenous Helong coastal polity and settlement name in West Timor

b_IDO_Kupang.etymology_analysis: Historic Helong port and polity name on Kupang Bay in West Timor, traditionally associated with the pre-colonial Helong ruler Nai Koepan; first documented in European records by the Dutch VOC in 1613 CE.

b_IDO_Sorbian.first_mention_attestation: 1515 CE, in early Portuguese accounts of Timor describing the island as divided between Sorbian (Servião) and Belos.
b_IDO_Sorbian.etymology_analysis: Early Portuguese exonym (Servião / Sorbian) for the western Timorese confederation under Sonba'i, attested from 1515 CE.

b_IDO_Roti.first_mention_attestation: 1756 CE, in Dutch East India Company (VOC) treaties with the rulers of Rote, Solor, and Sawu (following 16th-century CE Portuguese contact).
b_IDO_Roti.etymology_analysis: Island name (modern Indonesian Rote, older colonial Roti); local legend attributes it to a miscommunication between a Portuguese sailor and a fisherman named Rote.

b_IDO_Oetune.first_mention_attestation: Modern/vernacular coastal toponym in South Central Timor Regency; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_IDO_Oetune.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Uab Meto coastal toponym in South Central Timor (incorporating oe 'water'), unattested in historical sources before modern times.

b_IDO_Dili.first_mention_attestation: c. 1520 CE (recorded in early Portuguese accounts of northern Timor from c. 1520 CE onward, before becoming the capital of Portuguese Timor in 1769 CE)

morphemes.translation: coastal settlement and port name in northern Timor

b_IDO_Dili.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Timorese coastal port toponym on the northern shore of Timor, first noted in Portuguese maritime accounts around 1520 CE and established as the colonial capital in 1769 CE.

b_IDO_Insana.first_mention_attestation: Early 20th century CE, in Dutch East Indies administrative records of Swapraja Insana in North Central Timor.
b_IDO_Insana.etymology_analysis: Traditional Atoni domain (swapraja) in North Central Timor; unattested in written records prior to the colonial era.

b_IDO_Noimuti.first_mention_attestation: 1769 CE, in a Portuguese colonial source listing 'Nammutte' (Noimuti) among the realms of Servião.
b_IDO_Noimuti.etymology_analysis: From Uab Meto noi ('river') + muti ('white'), referring to a former Portuguese enclave in West Timor ceded to the Netherlands in 1904 CE.

b_IDO_Lahoasupala.first_mention_attestation: Modern/vernacular Fataluku name (Lohoasupala) for Lospalos in eastern Timor; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_IDO_Lahoasupala.etymology_analysis: Variant spelling of Fataluku Lohoasupala, the indigenous name of Lospalos in Lautém, East Timor; unattested before modern times.

b_MAL_Bacan.first_mention_attestation: 1512–1515 CE, in early Portuguese accounts and Tomé Pires's Suma Oriental documenting the spice-trading realm of Bacan.
b_MAL_Bacan.etymology_analysis: Name of one of the four royal centers of North Maluku (Maloko Kie Raha), first attested in early 16th-century CE Portuguese sources.

b_MAL_Weda.first_mention_attestation: Vernacular town and bay name in Central Halmahera; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_MAL_Weda.etymology_analysis: Vernacular South Halmahera toponym for the coastal town and bay in Central Halmahera Regency, unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_MAL_Obi.first_mention_attestation: 17th century CE, in Dutch East India Company (VOC) and European Maluku records.
b_MAL_Obi.etymology_analysis: Name of the main island in the Obi archipelago (also called Obira) south of Halmahera; lacks any pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_MAL_Ternate.first_mention_attestation: 1512 CE, when Portuguese explorers arrived in Ternate (earlier 1365 CE Nagarakretagama mentions 'Maloko', denoting Maluku broadly rather than the name Ternate).

morphemes.translation: island and sultanate name (earlier Kingdom of Gapi)

b_MAL_Ternate.etymology_analysis: Indigenous North Maluku island and polity name (originally Kingdom of Gapi), attested in external written records from 1512 CE.

b_MAL_Jailolo.first_mention_attestation: 1514 CE, in Portuguese accounts and Tomé Pires's Suma Oriental (c. 1515 CE) recording contact with Jailolo.

morphemes.translation: bay, polity, and historical name of Halmahera

b_MAL_Jailolo.etymology_analysis: Historical North Halmahera kingdom (Jika ma-kolano, 'Ruler of the Bay'), one of the four Maluku kingdoms, first documented in 1514 CE Portuguese records.

b_MAL_Golea.first_mention_attestation: Modern/vernacular locality in North Halmahera near Mount Dukono; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_MAL_Golea.etymology_analysis: Vernacular North Halmahera coastal settlement name north-northwest of Mount Dukono, lacking any pre-867 CE attestation.

b_MAL_Tidore.first_mention_attestation: 1512 CE, in early Portuguese accounts (and 1521 CE in Antonio Pigafetta's account of the Magellan expedition).
b_MAL_Tidore.etymology_analysis: Indigenous North Maluku island and sultanate name, documented in European sources from 1512 CE onward.

b_MAL_Koye.first_mention_attestation: Vernacular North Maluku toponym; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_MAL_Koye.etymology_analysis: Vernacular North Maluku settlement name associated with Tidore/Halmahera; no pre-867 CE written record exists.

b_MAL_Wasile.first_mention_attestation: Modern/vernacular district name in East Halmahera Regency, North Maluku; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_MAL_Wasile.etymology_analysis: Vernacular East Halmahera toponym facing Kao Bay, unattested in written sources prior to modern times.

b_MAL_Buru.first_mention_attestation: 1521 CE (explicitly recorded as Buru by Antonio Pigafetta during the Magellan expedition; the earlier 1365 CE Nagarakretagama refers to the island as Hutan Kadali)

morphemes.translation: indigenous name of Buru Island in Maluku

b_MAL_Buru.etymology_analysis: Name of Buru Island in the Maluku archipelago, first explicitly recorded under the name Buru by Antonio Pigafetta in 1521 CE (earlier called Hutan Kadali in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama).

b_MAL_Sula.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE, in early Portuguese/Ternate historical records documenting Ternate's expansion over the Sula Islands.
b_MAL_Sula.etymology_analysis: Indigenous name of the Sula archipelago between Sulawesi and Buru, first documented in the 15th–16th centuries CE.

b_MAL_Waisai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; coastal locality on southern Waigeo Island in Raja Ampat, West Papua, developed as the regency capital after 2003 CE

morphemes.translation: local coastal settlement name on Waigeo Island

b_MAL_Waisai.etymology_analysis: Local Raja Ampat coastal toponym on the southern shore of Waigeo Island in Southwest Papua, unattested prior to the modern administrative era.

b_MAL_Misool.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE, in early European and Tidore-era Maluku records.
b_MAL_Misool.etymology_analysis: From the Ma'ya language meaning 'port' or 'harbor', commemorating the arrival of the first king from Waigeo (original Matbat name: Batan Mee).

b_MAL_Ambwan.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (explicitly attested as Ambwan in Canto 14, verse 5 of Mpu Prapanca's Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama, naming Ambon within Majapahit's eastern maritime network)

morphemes.translation: historical form of Ambon (folk-etymologized via embun / ombong 'mist, dew')

b_MAL_Ambwan.etymology_analysis: Old Javanese form of Ambon Island in Maluku, attested in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama (Canto 14.5) alongside Wandan (Banda) and Maloko (Maluku); locally connected by folk etymology to embun/ombong ('dew/mist').

b_MAL_Wahai.first_mention_attestation: Modern/vernacular coastal settlement name on northern Seram Island; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_MAL_Wahai.etymology_analysis: Vernacular coastal town name on the north shore of Seram Island, unattested prior to 867 CE.

b_MAL_Waru.first_mention_attestation: 1779 CE, in Dutch colonial records as the base on eastern Seram of Prince Nuku's rebellion against the VOC.
b_MAL_Waru.etymology_analysis: Coastal settlement in eastern Seram named after the waru tree (Hibiscus tiliaceus), historically attested in 1779 CE during Prince Nuku's revolt.

b_wokam.first_mention_attestation: 1623 CE (recorded in Dutch East India Company treaties negotiated by Jan Carstenszoon with the leaders of Wokam / Wokan Island in the Aru archipelago in 1623 CE)

morphemes.translation: indigenous name of Wokam Island and its historic coastal trading center

b_wokam.etymology_analysis: Indigenous toponym of Wokam (Wokan) Island and its historic trading settlement in the northern Aru Islands, Maluku; first documented in Jan Carstenszoon's 1623 CE VOC treaty records.

b_trangan.first_mention_attestation: Vernacular island name in the southern Aru archipelago; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_trangan.etymology_analysis: Indigenous name of the largest and southernmost island of the Aru group, unattested in written records before the colonial period.

b_kaimana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; port town and historic petty kingdom on the Kowiai/Bomberai coast of West Papua, documented in 19th-century CE Dutch colonial records under Tidore suzerainty

morphemes.translation: coastal port and local polity name in southern West Papua

b_kaimana.etymology_analysis: Coastal port town and traditional petty kingdom (Kerajaan Komisi / Kaimana) on the southern Bird's Neck / Bomberai coast of West Papua, unattested prior to the early-modern/colonial era.

b_weri.first_mention_attestation: Vernacular settlement name in Tunas Gain Bay (Fakfak/Kaimana) associated with the Kingdom of Kaimana; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_weri.etymology_analysis: Vernacular settlement in Tunas Gain Bay where the Kingdom of Kaimana established its early capital; no pre-867 CE written record.

b_namatota.first_mention_attestation: 1828 CE, in Dutch colonial records when Fort Du Bus was constructed in Lobo, Namatota (Kaimana).

morphemes.translation: island and kingdom name in Kaimana

b_namatota.etymology_analysis: Name of an island settlement and Islamic kingdom in Kaimana Regency, first documented in 1828 CE Dutch colonial records.

b_timika.first_mention_attestation: Modern 20th-century CE town name in Mimika Regency, Central Papua; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_timika.etymology_analysis: Modern town name in Central Papua (Mimika Regency), unattested in historical sources prior to the 20th century CE.

b_asmat.first_mention_attestation: 1953 CE, when Catholic missionaries established the first permanent post among the Asmat people in southwestern New Guinea.
b_asmat.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Asmat people of South Papua, first brought into sustained external written records in the mid-20th century CE (1953 CE).

b_mapi.first_mention_attestation: Modern river and regency name (Mappi Regency created 2002 CE) in South Papua; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_mapi.etymology_analysis: Named after the Mappi River in South Papua; lacks any written attestation prior to the modern era.

b_dolok.first_mention_attestation: Modern/vernacular name for Kolepom / Yos Sudarso Island in South Papua; no pre-modern written attestation.
b_dolok.etymology_analysis: Vernacular island name (also called Kolepom, Kimaam, and formerly Frederik Hendrik Island) in South Papua, unattested before modern times.

b_soren.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; indigenous Biak-Numfor coastal toponym Soren in the western Bird's Head region of West Papua, the linguistic source of modern Sorong
b_soren.etymology_analysis: From the Biak-Numfor word soren ('deep and wavy ocean'), applied by seafaring Biak migrants to the western tip of the Bird's Head Peninsula in West Papua and later phonetically adapted by Maluku and European traders as Sorong.

b_maybrat.first_mention_attestation: Modern ethnolinguistic and administrative name (Maybrat Regency formed 2008 CE) in Southwest Papua; no pre-modern written attestation.

morphemes.translation: ethnolinguistic group of the central Bird's Head Peninsula

b_maybrat.etymology_analysis: Modern ethnolinguistic and regency name of the central Bird's Head Peninsula, Southwest Papua; no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_bintuni.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; vernacular West Papuan settlement and bay name on the Bird's Head Peninsula (known as Steenkool during the Dutch colonial period)
b_bintuni.etymology_analysis: Vernacular West Papuan toponym (known as Steenkool during the Dutch colonial period) on Bintuni Bay in the Bird's Head Peninsula, unattested prior to modern times.

b_amami.first_mention_attestation: 657 CE in the Nihon Shoki as Amami-shima (海見嶋, 'Amami Island'), followed by 682 CE (Amami-bito) and 699 CE in the Shoku Nihongi as Amami (菴美).

morphemes.translation: indigenous island name, possibly cognate with Ryukyuan creator deity Amamikyu

b_amami.etymology_analysis: First recorded in the Nihon Shoki under 657 CE as Amami-shima (海見嶋) and in 699 CE in the Shoku Nihongi as Amami (菴美), later standardized as 奄美. The name is traditionally linked to Amamikyu, the creator goddess in Ryukyuan mythology.

b_simajiri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Okinawan Simajiri / Japanese Shimajiri (島尻), the southern district of Okinawa Island corresponding to the 14th–15th century CE Nanzan kingdom and attested in the 16th–17th century Omoro Sōshi
b_simajiri.etymology_analysis: Okinawan Simajiri (Japanese Shimajiri 島尻, literally 'island's rear/tail'), naming the southern region of Okinawa Island associated with the Sanzan-period kingdom of Nanzan (Shimajiri-Ōzato Castle) and recorded in the Omoro Sōshi.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tōdaiwajō Tōseiden (779 CE, recording Jianzhen's 753 CE voyage to 阿児奈波 / Akinaha)
older_name_by_867.notes: Okinawa Island itself is attested as Akinaha (阿児奈波) in Jianzhen's 753 CE voyage account, prior to the post-867 Sanzan-period district name Simajiri (Shimajiri).

b_nakajan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; as Nakagami-hō (中頭方, Okinawan: Nakajan), the central district of Okinawa Island emerged during the Sanzan period (14th–15th centuries CE) and Ryukyu Kingdom administration.
b_nakajan.etymology_analysis: Nakajan is the Okinawan pronunciation of Japanese Nakagami (中頭, literally 'middle head'), denoting the central region of Okinawa Island corresponding to the Chūzan kingdom of the 14th-century Sanzan period.

b_kunjan_ucinaa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Kunigami (国頭, Okinawan: Kunjan) appears in post-867 Ryukyuan chronicles (such as Chūzan Seikan, 1650 CE) in connection with the 14th-century Hokuzan polity and 16th-century Ryukyu Kingdom administration.
b_kunjan_ucinaa.etymology_analysis: Kunjan is the Okinawan reading of Kunigami (国頭, 'head of the country'), designating the northern region of Okinawa Island historically associated with the Hokuzan kingdom during the Sanzan period.

b_SUL_Bhauu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Bhauu / Baubau is the historic royal port and fortified seat (Wolio) of the Sultanate of Buton on Buton Island, Southeast Sulawesi (Buton itself is first attested in 1365 CE)

morphemes.translation: historic fortified port and settlement name on Buton Island

b_SUL_Bhauu.etymology_analysis: Wolio/Butonese toponym (spelled Bhauu / Baubau) for the principal port and royal center adjacent to the Wolio fortress on Buton Island in Southeast Sulawesi, emerging in the early-modern Buton Sultanate era.

b_SUL_Goram.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (Canto 14) as 'Gurun', identified with the Gorom/Gorong archipelago in eastern Indonesia.

morphemes.translation: indigenous archipelago name (rendered 'Gurun' in Old Javanese)

b_SUL_Goram.etymology_analysis: Goram (also Gorom or Gorong) refers to the island group between Seram and Watubela in Maluku, mentioned in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama as 'Gurun' and later described by Alfred Russel Wallace in 1869 CE as 'Goram'.

b_SUL_Muna.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; local chronicles place the founding of the Muna (Wuna) kingdom in the 14th century CE (c. 1332–1371 CE), and Dutch/VOC records document it from the 17th century CE.

morphemes.translation: flower (from the folk etymology 'kontu kowuna', flowering stone)

b_SUL_Muna.etymology_analysis: Muna (local form: Wuna) is an island off southeastern Sulawesi. Although Liang Metanduno cave on Muna preserves Paleolithic rock art, the toponym Muna/Wuna has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Tukangbesi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the name 'Toekang Besi Eilanden' ('Blacksmith Islands') was recorded in Dutch colonial accounts and Malay sources in the early modern period.
b_SUL_Tukangbesi.etymology_analysis: Tukangbesi (modern Wakatobi Islands) literally means 'blacksmith' in Malay/Indonesian, reportedly applied by early Dutch/European visitors who observed widespread ironworking on the islands, or derived from a local polity name Tukabessi.

b_SUL_Rahambuu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; historic Tolaki / Western Bungku-Tolaki settlement, dialect, and local polity in Southeast Sulawesi associated with the Konawe/Mekongga sphere

morphemes.translation: indigenous toponym and dialect group name in Southeast Sulawesi

b_SUL_Rahambuu.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Bungku-Tolaki toponym and dialect/polity designation in Southeast Sulawesi (Kolaka/Konawe cultural sphere), documented only in modern linguistic and historical sources.

b_SUL_Kendari.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Kendari Bay appears on 16th-century Portuguese charts as 'Baia du Tivora' / 'Citta dela Baia', and the name Kendari was established in the 19th–20th centuries CE.

morphemes.translation: bamboo-and-wood pole used to push boats away from a dock

b_SUL_Kendari.etymology_analysis: Kendari is thought to derive from 'kandai', a Tolaki term for a bamboo-and-wood pole used to push boats from a landing. The settlement became the capital of Laiwoi and later Southeast Sulawesi in the 20th century CE.

b_SUL_Kolaka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the Mekongga kingdom in the Kolaka area is dated in local tradition to the 13th century CE and documented in 19th–20th-century Dutch colonial records.

morphemes.translation: indigenous coastal settlement and regency name

b_SUL_Kolaka.etymology_analysis: Kolaka is the main coastal town of the Tolaki Mekongga region in Southeast Sulawesi. Neither Kolaka nor Mekongga has any contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Wowoni.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; documented only in post-867 Butonese, Dutch colonial, and modern Indonesian administrative records.
b_SUL_Wowoni.etymology_analysis: Wawonii (formerly spelled Wowoni) is an island off Southeast Sulawesi. In the local Wawonii language, 'wawo' means 'high ground/above' and 'nii' means 'coconut' ('coconut highland/mountain').

b_SUL_Polean.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Polean / Poleang is a historic Moronene territory and coastal district in Bombana, Southeast Sulawesi, documented in early-modern Buton and Dutch colonial records

morphemes.translation: indigenous coastal territory and district name in Southeast Sulawesi

b_SUL_Polean.etymology_analysis: Moronene toponym (modern Poleang) in Bombana, Southeast Sulawesi, historically one of the principal Moronene domains linked to the Sultanate of Buton from the 17th century CE onward.

b_SUL_Kabaena.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; documented in early modern Dutch maritime records (such as the 1650 CE VOC fleet stranding near Kabaena) and Buton Sultanate histories.

morphemes.translation: indigenous island name (also known locally as Tokotua)

b_SUL_Kabaena.etymology_analysis: Kabaena (also called Tokotua) is a large island off the southeastern peninsula of Sulawesi. It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Tamboa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; locality in Central Sulawesi within the Bungku / Tambuku coastal sphere, unrecorded in pre-colonial primary sources
b_SUL_Tamboa.etymology_analysis: Local Austronesian toponym in eastern Central Sulawesi (Bungku/Tambuku region), lacking pre-modern primary source attestation.

b_SUL_Pano.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; no contemporary pre-867 written record exists for this Central/Southeast Sulawesi holding.
b_SUL_Pano.etymology_analysis: Pano appears in the repository as a constituent holding of Tambuku (Bungku). It lacks any contemporary written attestation by 867 CE or documented historical monograph.

b_SUL_Towuti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Lake Towuti appears in Bugis/Luwu oral tradition and 19th–20th-century Dutch geographical surveys.

morphemes.translation: indigenous name of Sulawesi's largest tectonic lake

b_SUL_Towuti.etymology_analysis: Towuti directly adopts the name of Lake Towuti (Danau Towuti), the largest lake on Sulawesi, located in the Malili lake system. It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Amparita.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; historic Bugis town in the Kingdom of Sidenreng (Sidenreng Rappang, South Sulawesi), documented in 17th-century CE Bugis lontara traditions as the sanctuary of the Tolotang community

morphemes.translation: historic Bugis settlement name in Sidenreng Rappang

b_SUL_Amparita.etymology_analysis: Historic Bugis settlement name in Sidenreng Rappang (South Sulawesi), famed in Bugis oral and lontara history since the 17th century CE as the cultural center of the pre-Islamic Towani Tolotang community.

b_SUL_Tosora.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Tosora developed as a settlement and capital of the Wajo Kingdom between the 15th and 17th centuries CE (documented in Lontara chronicles and 1670 CE VOC records).

morphemes.translation: indigenous settlement and former Wajo capital name

b_SUL_Tosora.etymology_analysis: Tosora in Wajo Regency, South Sulawesi, served as the fortified capital of the Bugis Kingdom of Wajo from the late 16th century until its fall to VOC and Bone forces in 1670 CE.

b_SUL_Lemo_Lemo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Lemo-Lemo appears in South Sulawesi Lontara traditions and early modern maritime/pinisi shipbuilding history (19th–20th centuries CE).
b_SUL_Lemo_Lemo.etymology_analysis: Lemo Lemo (Lemo-Lemo) is a coastal shipbuilding village in Bulukumba (also mentioned in Ajatappareng Lontara accounts), from Austronesian/South Sulawesi 'lemo' ('citrus'). It has no pre-867 written attestation.

b_SUL_Tamala.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; coastal locality in the Mamuju / West Sulawesi region, unrecorded in pre-colonial primary sources

morphemes.translation: local coastal toponym in West Sulawesi

b_SUL_Tamala.etymology_analysis: Local Austronesian toponym in the Mamuju region of West Sulawesi, lacking pre-modern historical attestation.

b_SUL_Tipor.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; no contemporary pre-867 written record exists for Tipor.
b_SUL_Tipor.etymology_analysis: Tipor is a constituent holding of Sampaga in the repository. It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE or documented historical entry.

b_SUL_Makassar.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE (explicitly attested as Makasar in Canto 14, verse 3 of Mpu Prapanca's Old Javanese Kakawin Nagarakretagama as a major polity and port in South Sulawesi)

morphemes.translation: having a lofty/great spirit, or manifest/open (ethnonym and port name)

b_SUL_Makassar.etymology_analysis: From Makassarese Mangkasara', the ethnonym and major port city of South Sulawesi (capital of the Gowa-Tallo maritime realm); first documented in the 1365 CE Old Javanese Nagarakretagama as Makasar.

b_SUL_Bungoro.first_mention_attestation: 1542 CE (visited by Portuguese ships 1542–1548 CE as part of the Siang heartland at Sengkae in modern Bungoro).
b_SUL_Bungoro.etymology_analysis: Bungoro is a district in Pangkajene and Islands Regency, South Sulawesi, encompassing the former capital site of the Kingdom of Siang. Its Makassar name derives from 'bungur' (the giant crape-myrtle tree).

b_SUL_Bantaeg.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (Canto 14) as 'Bantayan', listed alongside Luwuk and Makassar.

morphemes.translation: indigenous coastal polity name in southern Sulawesi

b_SUL_Bantaeg.etymology_analysis: Bantaeng (repository: Bantaeg; Dutch: Bonthain) is an ancient Makassar polity on the southern tip of Sulawesi, first attested in writing in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama as 'Bantayan'.

b_SUL_Boni.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Bugis Lontara chronicles place the founding of the Bone state around 1300 CE, and European/VOC records document it from the 16th–17th centuries CE.

morphemes.translation: indigenous Bugis kingdom and town name (historically 'sand' or coastal settlement)

b_SUL_Boni.etymology_analysis: Bone (repository: Boni) was the premier Bugis kingdom of eastern South Sulawesi, founded according to Lontara chronicles around 1300 CE and rising to regional hegemony under Arung Palakka in the 17th century CE.

b_SUL_Donggala.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; historic port town of the Banawa kingdom on Palu Bay in Central Sulawesi, documented in 17th–19th century CE Kaili, Bugis, and Dutch VOC records

morphemes.translation: historic port settlement name on Palu Bay

b_SUL_Donggala.etymology_analysis: Kaili toponym of the major historic trading port on the western shore of Palu Bay in Central Sulawesi, serving as the maritime gateway of the Banawa kingdom in the early-modern and colonial periods.

b_SUL_Parigi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the Kingdom of Parigi on the Gulf of Tomini existed from the 16th century CE and was fortified by the Dutch VOC in the 17th century CE.
b_SUL_Parigi.etymology_analysis: Parigi is a coastal polity and town on the Gulf of Tomini in Central Sulawesi, documented from the 16th–17th centuries CE as a regional kingdom and VOC trading post.

b_SUL_Donda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Dondo (Donda) in Tolitoli Regency is documented only in modern/colonial Indonesian administrative records.

morphemes.translation: indigenous ethnonym and district name in Tolitoli

b_SUL_Donda.etymology_analysis: Donda (standard Indonesian: Dondo) refers to the Dondo ethnic group and district in Tolitoli Regency, Central Sulawesi. It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Gorontalo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Gorontalo city and sultanate date back roughly 400 years to the 16th century CE, entering Dutch VOC records in the 17th century CE.

morphemes.translation: valley of the noble, or three mountains (Huidu Totolu)

b_SUL_Gorontalo.etymology_analysis: Gorontalo (repository: Gorontâlô) is a Dutch adaptation of local Hulontalo, variously derived from Hulontalangi ('valley of the noble' or 'inundated land') or Huidu Totolu ('three mountains'). Written attestations begin in the early modern period.

b_SUL_Suwawa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written records by 867 CE; although Gorontalo oral tradition places an ancestral Kingdom of Suwawa in the 8th century CE, written documentation begins in the early modern/Dutch colonial era.

morphemes.translation: indigenous ethnonym and ancestral kingdom name in Gorontalo

b_SUL_Suwawa.etymology_analysis: Suwawa is regarded in Gorontalo oral tradition as the oldest of the five pohala'a kingdoms ('Tiyombu'), with legendary 8th-century CE origins, but it lacks any contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Kali.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; mentioned in post-15th-century South Sulawesi Lontara chronicles (as a northern Sulawesi locality raided by Suppa/Sawitto alongside Kaili and Tolitoli).

morphemes.translation: indigenous settlement name (or variant of Kaili)

b_SUL_Kali.etymology_analysis: Kali appears in the repository as a constituent holding of Gorontalo, and in Bugis Lontara sources alongside Kaili and Tolitoli. It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Bolango.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the Kingdom/Sultanate of Bolango is dated in local historiography to 1482 CE and documented in Dutch VOC archives.

morphemes.translation: indigenous river, ethnonym, and kingdom name in Gorontalo

b_SUL_Bolango.etymology_analysis: Bolango is both a major river in Gorontalo (beside which the Gorontalo kingdom began) and one of the five pohala'a kingdoms (founded 1482 CE per local tradition). It has no written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Wenang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Wenang (modern Manado) appears in 16th-century Portuguese accounts and 17th-century Dutch/Bolaang Mongondow records (e.g., 1694 CE).
