morphemes.translation: indigenous Tombulu settlement name (associated with the wenang tree / kolintang wood)

b_SUL_Wenang.etymology_analysis: Wenang is the indigenous Tombulu Minahasan name for the mainland settlement that became modern Manado, attested from the 16th-century Portuguese and 17th-century Dutch colonial periods.

b_SUL_Bolaang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the Kingdom of Bolaang (later Bolaang Mongondow) is dated in local tradition to 1320 CE and documented in 17th-century Dutch VOC records (1670 CE).

morphemes.translation: enlightened by sunlight piercing the forest canopy (or from bolango 'sea')

b_SUL_Bolaang.etymology_analysis: Bolaang was the coastal seat of the Kingdom of Bolaang Mongondow in North Sulawesi. In Old Mongondow, Bola'ang (Gola'ang) means 'illuminated by sunlight through the dense forest canopy' (alternatively linked to 'bolango', sea).

b_SUL_Sangihe.first_mention_attestation: 1521 CE in Antonio Pigafetta's account of the Magellan expedition as 'Sanghir', followed by 1581–1582 CE Spanish accounts.
b_SUL_Sangihe.etymology_analysis: Sangihe (Sangir) is an archipelago north of Sulawesi toward Mindanao, first recorded in European sources by Antonio Pigafetta in 1521 CE as 'Sanghir'. It has no pre-867 written attestation.

b_SUL_Banggai.first_mention_attestation: 1365 CE in the Old Javanese Nagarakretagama (Canto 14) as 'Banggawi', listed among the eastern territories.
b_SUL_Banggai.etymology_analysis: Banggai is first attested in writing in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama as 'Banggawi', referring to the Banggai archipelago and later Ternate-vassal kingdom off eastern Sulawesi.

b_SUL_Balantak.first_mention_attestation: 1682 CE in Dutch colonial descriptions of the Banggai Kingdom's mainland territories on the East Peninsula of Sulawesi.
b_SUL_Balantak.etymology_analysis: Balantak denotes an ethnic group and district at the eastern tip of Sulawesi's East Peninsula. In Balantak, 'bala' ('fence/fortress') + 'tak' ('us') means 'our defense'. Described as part of Banggai in 1682 CE.

b_SUL_Luwuk.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Luwuk on the East Peninsula (Banggai) is documented in early modern Islamic/Ternatean and Dutch colonial records (distinct from 'Luwuk' = Luwu Kingdom in the 1365 CE Nagarakretagama).

morphemes.translation: indigenous coastal town name on the East Peninsula

b_SUL_Luwuk.etymology_analysis: Luwuk is the capital of Banggai Regency on Sulawesi's East Peninsula (not to be confused with the Bugis Kingdom of Luwu in South Sulawesi). It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Tojo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; historic kingdom and coastal town on Tomini Bay in Tojo Una-Una, Central Sulawesi, traditionally founded in the 18th century CE and documented in 19th-century Dutch records

morphemes.translation: historic kingdom and coastal town name on Tomini Bay

b_SUL_Tojo.etymology_analysis: Name of the historic Tojo Kingdom and coastal settlement along the southern shore of Tomini Bay in Central Sulawesi (Tojo Una-Una), established in the 18th century CE.

b_SUL_Togian.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the Togian (Togean) Islands in the Gulf of Tomini are documented in early modern and Dutch colonial records.

morphemes.translation: indigenous archipelago and main island name in the Gulf of Tomini

b_SUL_Togian.etymology_analysis: Togian (also Togean) is an archipelago of 56 islands in the Gulf of Tomini, Central Sulawesi. It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Bunta.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Bunta in Banggai Regency is documented only in modern/colonial Indonesian administrative records.

morphemes.translation: indigenous coastal settlement and district name

b_SUL_Bunta.etymology_analysis: Bunta is a coastal district in Banggai Regency, Central Sulawesi, on the Gulf of Tomini. It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Poso.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; coastal town, river, and lake name in Central Sulawesi, documented in 19th-century CE Dutch colonial and missionary records

morphemes.translation: indigenous name of the Poso River, Lake Poso, and coastal town

b_SUL_Poso.etymology_analysis: Pamona/Bare'e hydronym and settlement name in Central Sulawesi, shared by the Poso River, Lake Poso, and the port town at the river's mouth on Tomini Bay.

b_SUL_Panga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; no contemporary pre-867 written record exists for this Central Sulawesi holding.
b_SUL_Panga.etymology_analysis: Panga is a constituent holding of Mori in the repository. It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE or documented historical entry.

b_SUL_Waya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; no contemporary pre-867 written record exists for Waya in the Mori/Poso region.

morphemes.translation: fence/weir (as in Pamona 'waya masapi', eel weir) or local settlement name

b_SUL_Waya.etymology_analysis: Waya is a constituent holding of Mori in the repository (in Pamona/Poso, 'waya' denotes a traditional riverine weir). It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Malangke.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; archaeological and historical early capital of the Kingdom of Luwu in North Luwu, South Sulawesi, flourishing c. 14th–17th centuries CE and recorded in Bugis lontara chronicles

morphemes.translation: historic royal capital toponym on the Gulf of Bone

b_SUL_Malangke.etymology_analysis: Bugis toponym of the early maritime and iron-working capital of the Kedatuan Luwu on the northern shore of the Gulf of Bone (North Luwu, South Sulawesi), thriving from the 14th century CE until the capital moved to Palopo in the early 17th century CE.

b_SUL_Palopo.first_mention_attestation: c. 1620 CE in Bugis/Luwu chronicles, when the capital of the Kingdom of Luwu was relocated from Malangke to Palopo under Sultan Abdullah.

morphemes.translation: indigenous town name (traditionally linked to a local sweet dish or post-1620 Luwu capital)

b_SUL_Palopo.etymology_analysis: Palopo became the capital of the Kingdom of Luwu around 1620 CE after Malangke was abandoned, and is the site of South Sulawesi's oldest surviving mosque. It has no pre-867 written attestation.

b_SUL_Ussu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Ussu appears as a sacred landing site (of Batara Guru) in the Bugis I La Galigo epic (whose extant manuscripts date to the early modern period).

morphemes.translation: indigenous coastal village and sacred site name in East Luwu

b_SUL_Ussu.etymology_analysis: Ussu is a village in Malili District, East Luwu, revered in Bugis mythology (I La Galigo) as the place where Batara Guru descended to earth. It lacks any contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.

b_SUL_Malili.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Malili in East Luwu is documented in early modern Bugis/Luwu records and 19th–20th-century Dutch colonial administration.

morphemes.translation: indigenous town and river-basin name in East Luwu

b_SUL_Malili.etymology_analysis: Malili is the capital of East Luwu Regency at the head of the Gulf of Bone, giving its name to the Malili lake system. It has no contemporary written attestation by 867 CE.
